summary:
Halfway to Mars, a crewmate grabs their chest and collapses. Earth is up to 22 minutes away, each way. The person who has to act is an astronaut, not a doctor.

Nabz (Arabic for "pulse") is built for that moment and for the ordinary days before it. Emergency guides open without signing in, including CPR in microgravity with a 110-beat metronome. Each day, an astronaut takes a three-minute reaction test and logs sleep, and Nabz compares the results with that person's own normal from their last 14 check-ins. A guided blood pressure check explains each step, why it matters, and what to do when a value looks wrong. Reminders tell the crew when a check is due.

Fixed rules in code make every call, each tied to a published source and a NASA Human Research Program risk. An optional small AI model on board can explain a card in plain words, but it never decides. Nabz adapts to the ISS, the Moon, Mars and a remote Antarctic station: who to call changes, the health limits do not.

We tested the rules on real NASA OSDR data (Inspiration4 crew blood counts) and on four simulated crew members. Everything works offline.

Try it: https://nabz-drab.vercel.app (Sara, code 4120).
details:
Halfway to Mars, a crewmate grabs their chest and collapses. Earth is up to 22 minutes away, each way. Whoever is closest has to act, and they are an astronaut, not a doctor.

That scene from the challenge video is where we started. Nabz (Arabic and Urdu for "pulse") is the health app the crew runs on board: for that moment, and for the ordinary days before it, when small changes give the first warning. Everything works with the network off.

Try it: nabz-drab.vercel.app (sign in as Sara, code 4120). Emergency mode opens without signing in. Code: github.com/HamzaKhanBUIC/nabz

What Nabz does

1. Emergency mode: open to anyone, one step at a time

The red Emergency button is on every screen, including the sign-in page, because nobody should need a password while a crewmate is on the floor. It asks one question first: is this for you or for a crewmate? Then it shows one short, first-person step at a time.

  • For a crewmate: collapsed or unresponsive, CPR in microgravity, seizure, suspected low blood sugar.
  • For yourself: bleeding cut, burn, eye injury or chemical splash, allergic reaction, feeling dizzy or about to faint.

The CPR guide plays a 110-beat-per-minute metronome and follows the spaceflight CPR guideline (Hinkelbein et al. 2020): start in the Evetts-Russomano position, switch to the reverse bear hug if it does not work. Each guide says who to alert first, in plain words: "Alert a crewmate now. Do not wait for Earth." We checked every instruction against its source and fixed the ones that were wrong in our first draft, such as flushing a chemical out of the eye for 15 minutes.

2. A daily check-in that knows your normal

Each day, an astronaut takes a three-minute reaction test (PVT-B, the brief vigilance test from Basner et al.) and logs their sleep. Nabz scores reaction speed, lapses and false starts, throws out broken sessions, and compares the result with that person's own normal from their last 14 check-ins. Every result lands in a clear zone (building, in zone, watch or act) with a trend chart showing their personal band. One astronaut's normal can be another's warning sign, so Nabz never judges anyone against a crowd average.

3. Measurements that teach while you take them

Astronauts are not doctors, so the guided blood pressure check walks through each step: what to avoid for 30 minutes before, where the cuff goes, how to anchor yourself in microgravity, and a built-in 5-minute rest timer. It also asks about warning symptoms such as chest pain or shortness of breath. It averages the readings, classifies them with the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, compares them with the astronaut's own normal, and gives exactly one next step: nothing to do, measure again in 5 minutes, or alert the crew. Resting heart rate and blood oxygen (SpO2) are checked alongside, each against a sourced cut-off.

4. One clear card instead of a wall of numbers

A fixed priority table picks one action card: what changed, why it matters, what to do, the facts used, and the sources, with "Decision support, not a diagnosis." on every card. Each card names the NASA hazard and Human Research Program risk it relates to, and a "5 hazards" page shows what Nabz watches for each of NASA's five hazards of spaceflight. Status is never shown by colour alone: every level has a label and an icon too.

5. It adapts to where the crew is

The Commander can switch the mission profile: ISS, Moon, Mars transit, Mars surface, or a remote Earth station (Concordia in the Antarctic winter). The delay to Earth, the time until a patient could reach a hospital, who leads care, and the escalation wording all change. The health limits never change. On the ISS the card says to call the flight surgeon now; on the way to Mars it says "Act now with the crew medical officer; tell Earth after."

6. Built for a crew, with privacy

  • Crew sign-in: each crew member signs in with their own code (stored only as a scrypt hash) and sees only their own records.
  • Crew health for the Medical Officer: a summary card for each crewmate who has chosen to share, and every person can see who looked at their summary and when.
  • Send to Earth: shows exactly which entries would be shared, and nothing leaves until the astronaut confirms.
  • Reminders say when the next check-in or measurement is due.
  • Short health routines (hands, tension, blood pressure) are linked from the cards they help with.
  • Radiation estimate: mission dose so far, from published daily rates (George et al. 2024, Artemis I), against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

7. AI that explains, but never decides

In a medical emergency, a guess is dangerous. In Nabz, rules in code make every call: scores, zones, red flags and which card to show. The coach answers follow-up questions about a card using only that card's facts and verified text, and gives a fixed "no source" reply otherwise. Optionally, a small AI model runs locally on board (qwen3:4b through Ollama, no internet) to put the explanation in plainer words. It only sees questions the rules can already answer, cannot change the severity or the sources, and if it is slow or missing, Nabz falls back to the fixed text in under 4 seconds.

Real data and real sources

  • Real NASA data: blood counts from the SpaceX Inspiration4 crew (NASA Open Science Data Repository, study OSD-569), kept unmodified, run through the same personal-baseline engine as our crew on the "Real astronaut data" page.
  • Simulated crew: four crew members (Sara, Mateo, Elena, Kenji) with 120 days of data from a seeded generator: the same seed gives byte-identical data every time. No real health records are used.
  • 30 published sources: NASA-STD-3001, the NASA Human Research Program, AHA/ACC and Red Cross first-aid guidelines, PVT-B studies, Artemis I and Curiosity radiation measurements, NASA and ESA communication papers. Every number in the app has a source, and anything we chose ourselves is labelled as a design choice.

How we worked: ideas first, in FigJam

Before any code, the three of us ran a UX workshop in FigJam. We mapped the problem from the astronaut's side, sketched the emergency flow, argued over which features earn their place, and decided how each one should solve a real moment on a mission. The ideas, the feature list and the design choices came from that board and from our own discussion. We used AI as a catalyst for research: finding and summarising papers and NASA material, which we then checked against the sources ourselves. See our workshop board: NABZ UX Workshop & Research (FigJam export)

How we built it

  • Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4.
  • Backend: Node 24, TypeScript, Express 5, with zod 4 checking every request before anything touches it. The server recalculates every score and ignores any score a browser sends.
  • Health rules: pure TypeScript with no network, clock or randomness inside, so the same input always gives the same answer.
  • Offline first: no runtime network calls, no API keys, no CDN links. Fonts and icons ship with the app.
  • Quality: 155 automated tests (Vitest), a gate that runs typecheck, lint and tests, and GitHub CI on every change. All 26 planned features pass.
  • Hosting: Vercel for the site and Render for the API, both on free plans.
  • 58 commits over the two hackathon days, all in the public repository.

What our team considered

  • Stress: in an emergency, people cannot read paragraphs. One step per screen, short sentences, big buttons.
  • Not a doctor: every measurement explains how, why, and what to do next.
  • Trust: rules, not AI, decide. Every card cites its source and says it is decision support, not a diagnosis.
  • Privacy: sharing is opt-in, and every look at a crewmate's data is logged where they can see it.
  • Accessibility: status is never colour alone, and the app works on phones and laptops.
  • No signal: Mars has 2 to 3 weeks of disrupted contact at solar conjunction, so nothing core depends on the network.

Why it matters on Earth too

A crew far from a hospital is not only a space problem. The same app, with the same rules, fits an Antarctic research station in winter, a ship at sea, or a remote village hours from a clinic: anywhere people must look after each other before help can arrive.

Team Nova Trio

  • Hamza Imran: backend, health rules and AI
  • Maryam Amjad: frontend
  • Ameni Besbes: UI/UX design, FigJam UX workshop and pitch

Nabz is a NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 project built with public NASA data. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. AI use during development is logged in AI-USAGE-LOG.md in the repository.
